title: Bodhisattva Vows 1
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley emphasizes that true practice involves living on the basis of reality, rather than just sitting meditation (zazen). They suggest that everyday activities like smiling at strangers, listening to others without judgment, and letting go of opinions can be examples of working with the vows of saving all beings and ending delusion. By paying attention to these practices in daily life, one can cultivate a more authentic expression of Buddha's way. This approach encourages us to embody the bodhisattva vow by extending our intentions equally to every being and place, rather than just focusing on formal meditation practice.

sentences.text: Well, good evening everybody and welcome.
It's nice to see you.
It's nice to be back after a little absence on my part.
Tonight I'm going to talk about the chant that we do after the dharma talk, which we'll be chanting in 15 minutes or so.
It begins with, *May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.* Then it goes into the four bodhisattva vows.
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.* Next week, Nancy's going to talk about the last two vows, so tonight I'll talk about the first line and the first two vows.
Now, I'm not someone who can put together a talk very quickly.
I have to think about what I'm going to talk about, even if it's an assigned topic like this one.
Then I have to do some reading and research, and writing takes me a long time too.
But I like doing them, in part because I always learn something from the process.
Sometimes from the reading, sometimes from examining or just reflecting on part of my practice, or how the topic applies to the practice.
That happened here as well.

The first thing that struck me was the word "intentions," which Webster's defines as *exertion of the mind, determination to act in a certain way.* Now, I think meditation practice has helped me enormously over the years to be more aware of my intentions, especially my intentions with speech and with actions.
If I'm lucky, before I speak or act, I have a little time to reflect: what's my intention, and what do I think is going to happen if I say this or do that?
What would the impact be?
And then also during and after speech and actions, noticing the impact.
So sometimes I can stop myself when I have doubts about what I'm about to say or do.
Because I'm paying more attention to what happens, I can try to repair damage or do better next time if I've made a mistake.
When I was younger, I paid very little attention to the impact of my speech and my actions, so I'm really grateful for the way practice has helped me pay attention to this.
It's made a big difference.
But actually, this isn't what came up for me about intention.
It's something else.
I found myself asking questions like, in general, what are my deeper intentions in life?
What do I want to pay attention to?
What do I want to give my energy to?
What really matters to me?
These are questions I've asked myself from time to time, but it's pretty hard to keep them in mind.
They keep getting shoved aside by just the day-to-day things in life.
You know, I have to go mow the lawn, or I have to go to work, or I have to pay my bills, or something like that.
So I really appreciated being reminded of these important questions, and in the last several weeks I found myself keeping them in mind a lot more often.
I don't have the answers to them, but I don't really think the answers are important so much as keeping the question in mind.
So I'm grateful that preparing for this talk brought these questions up for me and made it possible for me to think about them more than I usually do.
Paying attention also fits with the second step in the Eightfold Path, which is right view or right thought.
Thoughts are often the forerunner of actions, and according to the Buddha, what we think, along with what we say and how we act, creates karma.
So thoughts can be as important as what we do and what we say.
And intention certainly has an impact on speech, actions, and thinking.
Now for the vow part of these chants, I've been reading a couple of different books by Shohaku Okumura.
One is *Living by Vow*, and in that book he goes over most of the chants that we do here and explains their meaning.
The other book is *Realizing Genjokoan*, which is a book explaining some of Eihei Dogen's writings.
Shohaku Okumura is a Japanese priest in his mid-60s.
He was trained in Japan.
He came over to the U.S. around 30 years ago, and he worked for a while at the Minnesota Zen Center, and then founded his own center in Bloomington, Indiana.
He's an excellent writer, especially when it comes to the meaning of Dogen's writings.
He's been a Dogen scholar all of his life, starting when he was about 18.
So, the usual definition of a vow is a solemn promise, a personal commitment, a religiously binding promise made to God or a saint or a deity.
Usually it's a promise to perform some act or service or to make a gift.
And part of the definition of a bodhisattva, that is, one who seeks enlightenment through the practice of Buddhism, is living by vow rather than living by karma.
According to Okumura, karma involves habit and preferences and a ready-made system of values based on the culture that you're living in.
And I like the way he says this: living by vow is like a compass that shows the way towards Buddha.
Okumura talks about vow as a foundation for our life that's not moved so much by human sentiment.
We vow towards Buddha, towards something absolute and infinite.
Vows are our direction.
A bodhisattva vows to help others and stay behind in the world, not entering nirvana until everyone else has entered first.
Now, the bodhisattva vows in this chant are connected to the four noble truths.
The first truth is that there is suffering in the world, in our lives, and the vow is, I vow to save all beings.
The second truth is that suffering is caused by delusion, by misunderstanding how life really is, by clinging and aversion.
And the second vow is, delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
I remember a talk Norman Fischer gave a number of years ago about these four vows.
He said these vows are impossible to meet, they're unattainable.
No one can save all beings and end all suffering.
No one can get rid of delusion.
So he said you don't have to feel bad or guilty about not succeeding on the one hand, because no one can succeed all the time.
And on the other hand, since the work is never done, you never stop.
You just keep at it, day after day, year after year.
You don't ever give up.
It will never be finished.
And you do that in a way that is sustainable, because saving all beings includes each one of us.
So it's okay to live a healthy lifestyle, to take a rest, to take a break once in a while, to do this kind of work in a sustainable way.
It's really the only way to do it and to keep going.
Okumura says the same thing when he writes, *To vow to save all beings doesn't mean that we believe that we have the power to help all those who are in trouble.
Imagining that or so would be arrogant.
To save all beings means to be one with all beings.* Norman made a similar point in one of his talks about becoming a priest.
He had three recommendations for priests, which I think are wonderful recommendations for all of us, whether you're a priest or not.
The first one was to be humble, the second was to try to be helpful, and the third was to see everyone as Buddha.
So that's really the same thing as being one with all beings.
Realizing our oneness with all beings and all things is the work of a lifetime, and the work of several lifetimes really.
The same thing is true of becoming free from delusion.
Studying the obstacles that affect each one of us, and studying Buddha's teachings and trying to bring them into our daily life, is also the work of a lifetime, or more than a lifetime.
I'm going to quote something from *Living by Vow*, and then something from *Realizing Genjokoan*.
So first, from *Living by Vow*:
*Our practice is the whole of our life, not something special that we do only in the monastery or at a sesshin or a retreat or in this room.
These are important parts of our practice, but the Buddha taught us just to awaken to the reality of our lives and live on the basis of that reality.
And according to Dogen, our sitting is not part of our practice, but rather other activities are part of our zazen.*
Zazen, for those of you who don't know, just means sitting meditation.
So other activities are part of our zazen, basically our whole life.
This is what's meant by the phrase, our zazen is absolute.
And in *Realizing Genjokoan*, Okumura makes a similar point.
He says, *Delusion and enlightenment lie only within the relationship between self and others.
Delusion is not some fixed thing within our mind that, if eliminated, will be replaced by enlightenment.

As long as we are alive, we exist only within the relationship to everything that we encounter in our lives.* So delusion or enlightenment lie in our interactions with everything that we encounter at each moment, one moment after another after another.
I was thinking, what would be some day-to-day examples of trying to work with these first two vows, with saving all beings and ending delusion?
I thought about smiling at a homeless person and saying good morning instead of ignoring him or her.
Or picking up a piece of garbage and throwing it away instead of stepping around it.
Or listening really thoroughly to someone, especially if you don't like what they're saying or don't agree with what they're saying.
Just listening without, at the same time, thinking about how you're going to respond while you're trying to listen.
Giving them your full attention.
I think that would be an example of being one with all beings.
Working with delusions seems harder, maybe in part because they're hidden and hard to notice, and I'm sure we all have many delusions we're not even aware of.

So it would be interesting sometime to have a group discussion, maybe a sangha conversation, about working with these vows so that we could take advantage of each other's practice and each other's life experience.
When I thought about delusions for myself, one that I run into a lot is an opinion about how things ought to be.
What ought to be done?
When it ought to be done?
Who ought to do it?
That kind of thing.
Whether that applies to me or to other people or organizations like insurance companies or the government, I'm just loaded with opinions about them.
Just about everything.
So what I thought I would try to do to work with this is just notice what my opinions and preferences are and then see how things actually turn out.
When things don't happen the way I want them to, which is most of the time, what actually happens?
A lot of the time, nothing.
Life goes on, things are different than I thought they'd be, but really it doesn't make any difference.
And some of the time, things turn out better.
If somebody does something different or at a different time or in a different way than I would have, what do you know, it's a better result.
I've been trying to notice that.
I know that I'm not going to get rid of my opinions, they're always going to be there, but I've been trying to turn down the volume on them and also maybe keep them to myself more.
And that's been a good practice.
So I think these are some of the things that have come up for me in studying this material and preparing for this talk.

I like the idea of keeping at it, that this is work we do for our whole lives, and to do it in a sustainable way and to be kind to ourselves while we're at it: to notice our mistakes, to acknowledge our mistakes, to learn from our mistakes.
That's what you need to do, you don't have to beat yourself up.
And I think that when we pay attention to these vows in day-to-day life in our imperfect human way, the merit of Buddha's way is being expressed.
So that's what I wanted to say about this part of the chant.
Thank you very much for listening, and now I guess we can actually do the chant.
